page2_img_1.png.title: Three-cluster network illustrating strong community structure (Q=0.493)
page2_img_1.png.description: A schematic network divided into three detected communities (each circled by a dashed red boundary). Within each circle the white nodes are densely connected by dark edges, while only a few lighter gray edges span between the clusters, visually reflecting tighter intra-group ties and sparser inter-group ties. The figure is the paper’s illustrative example of a network with modularity Q = 0.493, showing how the modularity measure captures pronounced community separation in communication networks such as OSS mailing-list interactions.

page7_img_2.png.title: Modularity distribution for Ant (Apr–Jun 2006) with observed value
page7_img_2.png.description: Kernel density of modularity (Q) values from ~100,000 randomized graphs (degree-preserving rewiring) for the Ant project in April–June 2006 is plotted (x-axis: Modularity 0–1; y-axis: Probability Density). The null distribution is tightly concentrated around ~0.2–0.3 (peak density ≈10–11), while the observed modularity is shown as a blue point at about 0.55, well to the right of the bulk of the random distribution. This large separation indicates the observed community structure is extremely unlikely under the random-degree model (the paper reports significance far below p=0.001), supporting the claim that the Ant mailing-list network has genuine modular structure rather than one expected by chance.

page7_img_1.png.title: Boxplots of modularity distributions across five OSS projects
page7_img_1.png.description: Five side-by-side boxplots show the distribution of modularity (y-axis 0–1) measured for Ant, Apache, Perl, Postgres, and Python over the sampled time intervals. Postgres has the highest median (≈0.7) and relatively high upper quartile, Apache shows a wide spread with upper values near ≈0.78, Perl’s median is around ≈0.55 with a notable high outlier above 0.8, Ant’s median lies near ≈0.55, and Python’s median is lower (≈0.45) with a lower whisker close to ≈0.25. Because most medians exceed ~0.4 (and many observations exceed 0.3), the plot supports the paper’s finding that these projects exhibit moderate-to-strong community structure in their email networks.

page7_img_3.png.title: PostgreSQL modularity over time: product vs process topics
page7_img_3.png.description: Time-series line plot of modularity (range 0–1) for PostgreSQL developer email networks from ~1998 to ~2007, with a solid line for product-related messages and a dashed line for process-related messages. The product-topic curve is consistently higher (approximately 0.5–0.85) with peaks around 2001–2002 and again near 2005–2006; the process-topic curve is lower (roughly 0.25–0.5) but shows a rise toward ~0.6 near 2006–2007. Because modularity quantifies strength of community structure, the figure demonstrates that discussions that mention code artifacts (product topics) produce more strongly modular, tightly clustered subcommunities than process discussions over the examined period.

page8_img_2.png.title: Modularity scores for product vs process emails across five projects
page8_img_2.png.description: A five-column table (Apache, Ant, Python, Perl, Postgres) reports mean modularity values computed from social networks built using only product-related messages, only process-related messages, and all messages, plus the adjusted p-value of a paired Wilcoxon test and the percent of messages classified as product. In every project the modularity for product messages is substantially higher (Apache 0.548, Ant 0.534, Python 0.473, Perl 0.567, Postgres 0.679) than for process messages (0.337, 0.485, 0.312, 0.423, 0.425) or the full message set (0.325, 0.459, 0.293, 0.400, 0.420). The adjusted p-values (≤ 0.033, mostly 0.001) indicate these increases are statistically significant, and the %Product column shows the fraction of messages classified as product-related (range ~26%–64%, highest in Ant). This pattern supports the paper’s finding that community structure is stronger in product-focused discussions.

page8_img_3.png.title: Wilcoxon p-values for co-commit differences by project
page8_img_3.png.description: A one-row table listing Wilcoxon test p-values (after multiple-hypothesis correction) for five projects: Ant = 0.000, Apache = 0.052, Perl = 0.502, Postgres = 0.000, Python = 0.000. These p-values come from two-sample Wilcoxon tests comparing the number of files co-committed by pairs of developers within the same email subcommunity versus pairs from different subcommunities (testing Hypothesis 3). Interpreting p<0.05 as evidence of greater within-subcommunity collaboration, Ant, Postgres and Python show strong significance, Apache is marginal (0.052), and Perl shows no significant difference (0.502).

page5_img_1.png.title: Project dataset summary: dates, messages, participants, files, developers, commits
page5_img_1.png.description: Table of the mined data for five projects (Apache, Ant, Python, Perl, PostgreSQL) showing the archived date ranges and activity counts used in the study. For each project it lists begin/end dates (e.g., Apache: 1995-02-27 to 2005-07-13; Perl: 1999-03-01 to 2007-06-20) and totals for messages (Apache 101,250; Ant 73,157; Python 66,541; Perl 112,514; PostgreSQL 132,698), mailing-list participants (range: Python 1,329 to Perl 3,621), files in the repository (range: Apache 1,092 to Perl 13,308), developers with commit access (Python highest at 92), and commits (PostgreSQL 111,847; Perl 92,502; Ant 58,254). The table highlights that PostgreSQL and Perl have the largest message/participant volumes, Perl has the largest file count, and Python has the most developers, contextualizing the scale and heterogeneity of the projects analyzed.

page8_img_1.png.title: Perl developer mailing‑list subcommunity network (Apr–Jun 2007)
page8_img_1.png.description: A graph of email interactions among Perl project participants for April–June 2007 showing several distinct subcommunities (the partition for this snapshot has modularity Q≈0.76). Nodes are drawn as ovals for general participants and diamonds for developers, and rectangular boxes highlight the algorithmically detected subgroups; straight lines between nodes represent email replies or exchanges (edge weights used by the algorithm are not visually encoded). The layout reveals dense ties inside each boxed cluster and relatively few ties between clusters, with a small number of nodes acting as bridges linking otherwise separate groups—illustrating strong, modular community structure in product‑related discussion during this period.

page10_img_1.png.title: Python subcommunity: contributors, communications, and directories (Apr–Jun 2003)
page10_img_1.png.description: A network snapshot (April–June 2003) of a single Python mailing-list subcommunity: diamond nodes denote developers, ovals denote other participants, and rectangular boxes denote top-level directories those people committed to. Black edges inside the boxed group show the dense email interactions among the participants, while the red curved edges link those same actors to many different directories (for example /Modules/, /Objects/, /Lib/, /Lib/test/, /Include/, /Doc/ext/, /Lib/distutils/), indicating commits spread across the code tree. The diagram visualizes the paper’s case study where this cohesive social group collaborated on garbage-collection diagnosis and fixes that cut across both C interpreter modules and Python library files, i.e., a cross-cutting technical concern rather than a single localized module.
